summary:
Nāgāland stands under India's national framework on gender recognition, and no deviation from the national position has been identified for the state at a margin material enough to score separately (within ±0.02). A visitor to Nāgāland therefore faces the same recognition, documentation and policing conditions as elsewhere in India.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. The bill removes the right to self-identification affirmed by the Supreme Court's 2014 third-gender ruling, narrows the statutory definition of a transgender person, and mandates medical certification for identity recognition. It was approved by both houses and, on the sourcing available, awaits presidential assent.

The government argues that the narrower definition improves delivery of welfare schemes. Critics, and Human Rights Watch in its assessment of 26 March 2026, describe the amendment as a major reversal of the 2014 rights and a criminalisation of identity; the mandatory medical certification is characterised as an attack on privacy and dignity, and the exclusion sweeps in trans men, trans women, non-binary and gender-fluid people who self-identify outside the recognised categories.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have interpreted to cover gender identity: the Supreme Court has held that discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity falls within Article 15's prohibition of discrimination by sex, and the Allahabad High Court extended that in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on sexual orientation grounds. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been asked to take a medical exam by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card for identity verification. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic; victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans on conversion therapy from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Facilities and care access are largely set at state level, so the offer a visitor can actually use depends on which state they are in. Tamil Nadu and Kerala run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several other states, including Maharashtra and Odisha, provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras. Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community. In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Intersex minors remain at risk: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.
tangentialFactors:
Transitional care and welfare provision in India varies substantially between states, so conditions observed in Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra or Odisha do not travel: Nāgāland has no sourced welfare board of its own, and a visitor moving between states may find a scheme available in one and absent in the next.

The direction of national law and the direction of judicial protection are running opposite ways. The March 2026 amendment narrows statutory recognition while courts continue to read sex-based non-discrimination protections broadly, and while a foreign government's December 2025 assessment records police abuse as limited rather than systemic even as detainee testimony describes abusive treatment by railway police.

Activist and international scrutiny is unusually active around the current recognition regime. Human Rights Watch urged the president not to sign the amendment bill, and rights campaigners including Akkai Padmashali describe the change as an attack on the right to exist, which suggests continued public contestation rather than a settled position a visitor can rely on.

outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill has received presidential assent and entered into force is unresolved in the sourcing: one account describes it as passed by both houses, another as awaiting assent at the time of writing.

No Nāgāland-specific material was sourced on local policing practice, document issuance at state offices, or the presence of any state welfare board or transition-related healthcare capacity within the state. The conditions recorded here are national or drawn from other states and should not be read as findings about Nāgāland's own administration.

The divergence in police-conduct assessments is unresolved rather than reconciled: the UK policy note's finding of limited, non-systemic abuse and the June 2024 detainee interviews rest on different samples and are not resolved by any source available here.
